title: Iraq Crude Output Hits 2019 High of 4.6M Bpd as Brent Tops $96, Iran Drafts a Zero-Oil Budget, and Germany Eyes a €4B Urenco Buyout
subhead: Brent crude rebounded above $96 a barrel despite Iraqi production surging by 540,000 bpd to 4.6 million bpd in October; Tehran instructed ministries to prepare next year's state budget assuming zero oil revenue after halting crude loadings since August; and Berlin moved to acquire a €4 billion stake in uranium enricher Urenco.

sections.heading: Iraq Crude Output Surges to 4.6 Million Bpd as Brent Climbs Back Above $96
sections.body:
Iraq's crude oil production jumped by 540,000 barrels per day (bpd) from September to reach 4.6 million bpd in October—its highest output level since 2019—as flows through the Strait of Hormuz accelerated alongside production increases from Saudi Arabia and Kuwait, according to the International Energy Agency's monthly report cited by OilPrice. OPEC's second-largest producer capitalized on available export capacity even as baseline global demand forecasts softened (OilPrice, Anadolu Agency).

Despite the surge in Gulf supply, Brent crude climbed back above $96 a barrel in Friday trading as post-midterm optimism over a rapid Middle East peace settlement faded and geopolitical risk premiums returned to energy futures, OilPrice reported. Traders remained on edge over active fighting in Yemen and ongoing hostilities between Washington and Tehran.
sections.whyItMatters: Brent's climb back above $96 despite a 540,000 bpd Iraqi production jump demonstrates that war-risk premiums in the Persian Gulf are outweighing physical OPEC+ supply additions.

sections.heading: Iran Drafts Next Year's State Budget on Premise of Zero Oil Revenue
sections.body:
Iran is drafting next year's government budget under the assumption that state oil revenues could fall completely to zero, with senior Iranian budget official Mohammad Ghasemi instructing ministries on Monday to prepare for a fiscal scenario without crude receipts, OilPrice reported. According to IEA tanker-tracking data cited in the report, Iran has loaded no crude oil exports since August 25 amid wartime naval interdictions and infrastructure pressure.

Reflecting the depth of Tehran's fiscal squeeze, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Friday that there is 'no need' for further US military strikes on Iran because the economic pain on the country 'is so great' (The Times of Israel). Meanwhile, the White House confirmed to Reuters and CNA that President Donald Trump will discuss the Iran conflict alongside nuclear arms reductions during his trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin next week.
sections.whyItMatters: Planning a national budget around zero oil revenue confirms that halting Iranian crude loadings since late August has created an acute fiscal crisis in Tehran that Washington now views as its primary pressure tool.

sections.heading: Germany Plans €4 Billion Buyout of RWE and E.ON's Stake in Uranium Enricher Urenco
sections.body:
The German government is preparing to buy the combined one-third stake held by German utilities RWE and E.ON in nuclear fuel consortium Urenco for up to €4 billion, OilPrice reported citing German press disclosures. Under Urenco's treaty governance structure, the enrichment company is jointly owned by the British and Dutch states alongside the two German power companies.

According to OilPrice, London requested that Berlin purchase the stake directly to ensure ownership remains strictly in European governmental hands as Britain prepares to use Urenco enrichment facilities to produce fuel for its military nuclear reactors, including those powering Royal Navy submarines.
sections.whyItMatters: Berlin's planned €4 billion nationalization of RWE and E.ON's Urenco shares locks Western Europe's primary uranium enrichment capacity under direct sovereign control for both civilian power and defense propulsion.

sections.heading: Trump Extends Jones Act Tanker Waiver 90 Days as US Crude Hits Record and Senate Advances BAAJA Power Bill
sections.body:
US President Donald Trump extended a Jones Act shipping waiver for another 90 days on Friday, allowing foreign-flagged tankers to continue transporting crude oil and refined fuels between American ports as the war with Iran keeps domestic fuel costs elevated, a White House official confirmed to Reuters via OilPrice. On the production front, Baker Hughes data published Friday showed active US oil rigs held steady at 463—with total oil and gas rigs at 601, up 52 from a year earlier—as US crude output hit another all-time record, North Dakota operators planned output increases, and Northern Oil & Gas reached its first deal to acquire Canadian energy assets (OilPrice, EnergyNow, Hart Energy).

In domestic power markets, the US Senate approved a preliminary version of the Bipartisan Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), prompting warnings from energy analysts at OilPrice that the legislation could allow cash-rich AI technology giants to outmuscle regulated electric utilities for generation capacity and grid interconnections.
sections.whyItMatters: Extending the Jones Act waiver for 90 days while US crude output hits new records underscores that domestic refining and coastal transport bottlenecks—not wellhead production—remain Washington's main fuel-price vulnerability.

sections.heading: Indonesia Drops Commodity Export Monopoly Plan as US-China Rare Earth Truce Extends
sections.body:
Indonesia scrapped plans to establish a new state-owned enterprise as the sole exporter of its coal, palm oil, and ferroalloys, opting instead to mandate comprehensive export data reporting while leaving private commercial marketing intact, the South China Morning Post reported. The reversal relieved Asian coal and industrial metals buyers who had feared supply bottlenecks from one of the world's largest thermal coal and nickel-alloy suppliers.

In critical minerals and regional energy diplomacy, Washington and Beijing extended their rare-earth trade truce (Washington Examiner) while analysts at Benchmark Mineral Intelligence assessed how Democratic midterm gains in Congress could reshape US battery and mineral supply-chain subsidies. Meanwhile, OilPrice reported that Beijing's state broadcaster CGTN launched a broad information campaign in Central Asia's most populous state to counter Washington's expanding trade and energy partnerships across the Caspian and Central Asian corridor.
sections.whyItMatters: Jakarta's retreat from a state coal and ferroalloy export monopoly and the extension of the US-China rare-earth truce ease near-term disruption risks across Indo-Pacific energy and critical-mineral trade.

bottomLine: Energy markets on Saturday balanced surging physical production against wartime fiscal and logistical strains: Iraq boosted crude output by 540,000 bpd to a post-2019 high of 4.6 million bpd even as Brent rebounded above $96, while Iran began drafting a zero-oil-revenue budget after more than two months without crude loadings. Simultaneously, Germany moved toward a €4 billion buyout of RWE and E.ON's stake in uranium enricher Urenco, President Trump extended the Jones Act tanker waiver for 90 days, and Indonesia abandoned plans for a state export monopoly over coal, palm oil, and ferroalloys.
sources: OilPrice, South China Morning Post, Reuters, Times of Israel, CNA, EnergyNow, Hart Energy, Washington Examiner, Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, Anadolu Agency
